title: Polynomial-time quantitative stochastic parity verification
formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm deciding whether \[\sup_\sigma\inf_\tau\Pr^{\sigma,\tau}_v[\text{the least priority occurring infinitely often is even}]\ge q\] for every finite turn-based stochastic parity game and binary-encoded rational threshold q∈[0,1]?
definitions:
The input is a finite directed graph without dead ends. Vertices are partitioned into player Max, player Min, and random vertices. At a player vertex its owner chooses one successor; at a random vertex a rational probability distribution over successors is supplied explicitly. Probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one. Each vertex has a nonnegative integer priority written in binary. Play starts at a supplied vertex v and continues forever. The parity event is defined by the least priority visited infinitely often, so parity is independent of any finite prefix.

A strategy assigns a probability distribution over available moves to every finite observed history ending at that player’s vertex. Both players see the full history; memory and randomization are allowed. For fixed strategies the transition rules determine the probability of the parity event. The value displayed is the lower value for Max; the decision asks the non-strict comparison ≥q, including equality. Time is polynomial in the full bit length of graph, priorities, probabilities and threshold on a deterministic Turing machine. The number of priorities and probability denominators are unrestricted. Only this exact threshold decision is required, not printing exact game values or optimal strategies.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked polynomial-time threshold algorithm, or prove that none exists. Algorithms for deterministic parity games alone, qualitative thresholds alone, a fixed number of priorities, or approximate values without exact threshold control do not settle the question. Assumption-based hardness must be identified as conditional.
context: Chatterjee, Jurdziński and Henzinger study the turn-based stochastic parity model arising in verification and control. The quantitative question combines adversarial choices, probability and an infinite-play objective.
why: This combines randomness, adversarial control and infinite-run specifications in a central quantitative verification task.

This is the quantitative verification problem studied directly by Henzinger, Chatterjee and Jurdziński, combining adversarial control, randomness and infinite-run specifications.
